signals.title: @mirek_szczerba: Yes of course Elie. The term “Indian spy intelligence in space” refers to the rapid expansion of India’s military spy satellite and intellig
signals.content: Yes of course Elie. The term “Indian spy intelligence in space” refers to the rapid expansion of India’s military spy satellite and intelligence systems (Space-Based Surveillance – SBS), as well as its next-generation space technologies. India has undergone a transformation from hiding its military assets from foreign spy satellites to building one of the most advanced orbital surveillance networks in the world. The key pillars of Indian space intelligence include: Project SBS-III: A Mega-Constellation of 52 Satellites The Indian government's Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) approved a massive SBS-Phase III program valued at approximately INR 27,000 crore (around $3.2 billion). The Goal: Deploy 52 advanced spy satellites into Low Earth Orbit (LEO) and Geostationary Orbit (GEO). These satellites eliminate previous blind spots (such as a lack of nighttime visibility) and offer 24/7 real-time monitoring of borders, coastlines, and troop movements. They utilize advanced Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), high-resolution optics, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) for inter-satellite communication. Space Intelligence Warfare and "Bodyguard Satellites" India's new defense doctrine recognizes space as a direct theater of intelligence operations. To protect its billion-dollar space infrastructure, India is developing "bodyguard satellites." Detect and neutralize hostile inspector satellites. Counter cyberattacks and signal jamming in orbit. Private Sector Success in "In-Orbit Snooping" Private Indian companies are working closely with ISRO and the military to deliver breakthrough technologies. The private satellite AFR (80 kg) achieved an unprecedented feat by tracking and photographing the International Space Station (ISS) from orbit. This demonstrated India's capability to conduct surveillance on other space assets and hostile satellites (known as in-orbit snooping). This startup launched the MOSAIC system and the SCOT (Space Camera for Object Tracking) satellite—the first commercial Space Situational Awareness (SSA) solution capable of detecting objects as small as 5 cm. Existing Intelligence Network (EMISAT, RISAT, Cartosat) The new constellation will join currently operational systems, such as the RISAT radar series, the Cartosat optical series, and the EMISAT satellite (managed by the NTRO). EMISAT is responsible for electronic intelligence (ELINT), locating adversary radars and communication systems directly from space... @CedricLeighton #India #Espionage

signals.title: Quant-Arena: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Quantitative Trading Research
signals.content: Quantitative research is an iterative loop: a researcher proposes a market hypothesis, implements it as an executable signal, tests it on historical data, and decides what to keep. Existing benchmarks score formulas, code, or individual trading decisions, leaving open whether large language models (LLMs) can complete this loop and produce strategies that work beyond the research period. We introduce Quant-Arena, a benchmark and public leaderboard for end-to-end quantitative research on real A-share market data. A model constructs features and stock-scoring code, receives feedback only on 2022--2023, and freezes one strategy for assessment on the sealed year 2024. A cash-account evaluator applies trading constraints and costs, including market impact estimated from a simulated order book. Scores are dominated by realized excess return and complemented by signal quality and the diversity of features used by the strategy. We evaluate nine frontier models, among which GPT-6 Astra scores highest; yet no model beats the equal-weight market in 2024. Quant-Arena is open to submissions from any model or agent harness.
signals.score_reason: academic/research signal; agentic AI relevance; large language model relevance; model capability relevance. Final score: 87. Freshness: source age 0.93d.
signals.brief_en: Quant-Arena benchmarks LLM agents on end-to-end quantitative trading research using Chinese A-share market data. Models formulate hypotheses, generate feature/scoring code, and optimize strategies using 2022–2023 data before evaluation on a sealed 2024 dataset. The framework incorporates real-world trading constraints, execution costs, and order-book market impact. While GPT-6 Astra led among nine frontier models tested, no agent outperformed the equal-weight market benchmark in 2024, highlighting ongoing limitations in out-of-sample financial generalization.

signals.title: Parallel AI Agent Collaboration as Graph-Structured Distributed Block Optimization
signals.content: Parallel AI agents can produce useful local edits yet degrade a shared solution when their edits are combined. We model this coordination problem as discrete block optimization with an exactly evaluable objective and a known dependency graph. Independent sets certify compatible edits whose verified gains, measured against the same current solution, add exactly. A coordinator constructs a safe compatible candidate and can also evaluate interacting edits to capture favorable interactions. We prove that an optimal fractional coloring yields a merger that preserves a $1/χ_f(G)$ fraction of the total verified local improvement, where $χ_f(G)$ is the graph's fractional chromatic number. This guarantee is tight among mergers that select a subset of the same proposals. Under conditional local-improvement guarantees and a block error-bound condition, repeated collaboration converges geometrically in the objective gap. The rate separates task structure, agent allocation, and computation cost, yielding a linear program for agent assignment and an explicit time-cost trade-off. Code-repair experiments show that verified merging resolves conflicts between individually useful edits that cause naive merging to fail. On larger conflict-free tasks, parallel agents reduce modeled completion time at higher input-token-equivalent cost. On three public road networks, fractional integration retains 922 units of verified graph-cut improvement across 90 paired runs. For route-search agents sharing exclusive access to vehicle routes, fractional scheduling reduces measured wall time by a median of 15% across twelve paired runs, with route-cost changes varying across runs.

signals.title: TARSphere: A Robot-Oriented Full-Stack Framework for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents in Evolving Physical and Social Environments
signals.content: Robots must act under physical and social constraints while adapting to changes in their environment and human needs. Existing embodied-agent systems often focus on specified goals or abstract execution into symbolic actions, limiting evaluation in an evolving world. We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for physically and socially grounded long-horizon embodied agents. TARSphere-Infra runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue. An event-driven finite-state machine (FSM) uses completed actions and delivered information to update task states and evaluate outcomes. TARSphere-Harness, its embodied brain harness, lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) act through multi-level executable skills, using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback to revise its decisions. On this foundation, agent-in-the-loop curation aligns task semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry to construct TARSphere-Bench: 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes. Five paired conditions assess perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding for navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks. Our evaluation of 8 MLLMs shows that general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult. Frequent collisions and falls further motivate evaluating execution safety alongside task success, even with a shared action interface and decision budget.

signals.brief_en: TARSphere is a robot‑oriented full‑stack framework for long‑horizon embodied agents operating in dynamic physical and social settings. It combines a physics‑based simulator (TARSphere‑Infra) with NPCs and constrained dialogue, an event‑driven finite‑state machine for task‑state updates, and a brain harness (TARSphere‑Harness) that lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) execute multi‑level skills using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback. The framework supports the creation of TARSphere‑Bench, a benchmark of 360 episodes in 30 indoor scenes covering navigation‑and‑report and fetch‑and‑deliver tasks under five paired conditions: perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task updates, human coordination, and intent understanding. Evaluation of eight MLLMs shows that general‑purpose models can surpass specialized embodied models, but updating tasks and interacting with humans remain challenging, and safety issues such as collisions and falls are frequent, highlighting the need to assess execution safety alongside task success.

signals.title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping
signals.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) based on PPO-style clipping has become an effective approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, standard token-level clipping measures policy change only through the conditional probability of the current token, while the prefix conditioning context is itself generated by the policy. This mismatch becomes especially consequential in long-response and off-policy training. We reformulate autoregressive generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and derive its performance-difference identity under behavior-policy sampling. The resulting change of measure identifies the cumulative likelihood ratio of the generated prefix as the exact importance weight for each stepwise policy-improvement term. Starting from the monotonic-improvement principle of trust-region policy optimization, we then construct a prefix-level trust region using the exact reverse-KL coordinate $r-1-\log r$, whose behavior-policy expectation equals the corresponding prefix-distribution KL divergence. This yields EPIC, a PPO-style sequence-clipping method that directly regulates prefix-level policy drift without relying on a local quadratic approximation or expert-routing replay. Experiments on off-policy reinforcement learning with a sparse mixture-of-experts language model show that EPIC consistently outperforms standard and sequence-level clipping baselines across mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, while remaining competitive with routing-replay-based alternatives. Code is available at https://github.com/LiChengxi666/EPIC.

signals.title: Differentially Private Sparse Reward Estimation with Preference Feedback
signals.content: Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) has become a central paradigm for aligning Large Language Models with human values. However, the reliance on sensitive preference data necessitates rigorous differential privacy (DP) guarantees to prevent user information leakage. Existing private alignment methods typically assume dense reward parameterizations, resulting in estimation error bounds that scale polynomially with the ambient {model size $d$}. Such dependence is prohibitive in modern {overparameterized models} where $d$ is vast. In this work, we study \emph{Private Sparse RLHF} problem to address this limitation, assuming that human preferences (reward model) are governed by a subset of $s^* \ll d$ relevant features. We provide the first comprehensive theoretical framework for differentially private sparse reward estimation from pairwise preference feedback under the Bradley-Terry-Luce model, and introduce efficient algorithms for both Sample-DP and Label-DP settings. Theoretically, under the squared $\ell_2$ parameter estimation error, we establish upper bounds of $\widetilde{O}(s^*/n + {s^*}^2/n^2\varepsilon^2)$ for $(\varepsilon,δ)$-Sample-DP and $\widetilde{O}(s^*/n + s^*/n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon$-Label-DP based on randomized response, where $n$ is the training data size. For the lower bounds, we show that the Sample-DP rate is nearly optimal, and that the guarantee for our Label-DP method cannot be further improved within the randomized-response framework. We also provide a general lower bound for the problem with Label-DP. Empirically, our framework demonstrates superior efficacy over dense baselines across sentiment generation and safety alignment benchmarks, offering a significantly more favorable privacy-utility trade-off.

signals.brief_en:
Title: Differentially Private Sparse Reward Estimation with Preference Feedback

RLHF aligns large language models using human preference data, but such data are sensitive and require differential privacy (DP). Existing private methods assume dense reward models, leading to error bounds that grow with the full model dimension d, which is impractical for over‑parameterized systems. This work defines the Private Sparse RLHF problem, assuming the true reward depends on only s* ≪ d features. Under the Bradley‑Terry‑Luce pairwise‑preference model, we propose efficient algorithms for both Sample‑DP and Label‑DP. For squared ℓ₂ parameter error, the Sample‑DP algorithm achieves a rate ˜O(s*/n + s*²/(n²ε²)), while the Label‑DP method (randomized response) attains ˜O(s*/n + s*/(nε²)). Lower‑bound analysis shows the Sample‑DP rate is near‑optimal and the Label‑DP bound cannot be improved within the randomized‑response framework. These results demonstrate that privacy‑preserving reward estimation can scale with the intrinsic sparsity s* rather than the full dimension d, making DP‑RLHF feasible for large models.

signals.title: LongZero: Enhancing Long-Context Reasoning in LLMs from Zero Data
signals.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) is an effective way to strengthen the long-context reasoning of large language models (LLMs), but it needs training data that are long, diverse, challenging, and verifiable. Human annotation of such data is expensive, naturally occurring data are too scarce to sustain RL, and existing synthesis methods depend on external corpora or stronger teacher models, which become harder to obtain as the trained models get stronger. Recently, RL from zero data, in which a model learns from tasks it proposes itself, has achieved excellent performance, but existing methods target short-context tasks. Therefore, we propose $\textbf{LongZero}$, a method that lets an LLM improve its own long-context reasoning without any external data. Instead of writing questions and answers over existing documents, LongZero first has the model synthesize the question and answer with its supporting evidence in a compact structured form, and only then separately expands the evidence into a long multi-document context. LongZero combines these self-written multi-hop reasoning tasks with self-written multi-round retrieval tasks and trains the model with GRPO. We evaluate LongZero on two LLMs across five long-context reasoning benchmarks and compare it with RL on data synthesized from external corpora. Experimental results show that LongZero can generalize to real tasks, and outperforms both baselines, suggesting a viable and promising path to improving long-context reasoning of LLMs.

signals.brief_en: LongZero is a zero‑data reinforcement‑learning approach that enables large language models to improve long‑context reasoning without external corpora. The method first has the model generate a compact, structured question‑answer pair with supporting evidence, then expands that evidence into a long multi‑document context. Using self‑created multi‑hop reasoning and multi‑round retrieval tasks, LongZero trains the model with GRPO. Evaluations on five long‑context benchmarks with two LLMs show that LongZero generalizes to real tasks and outperforms both standard RL on synthesized external data and baseline methods, indicating a promising path for enhancing long‑context capabilities.
